title: IS SEX ONLY FOR HAVING CHILDREN?
paragraphs:
IS SEX ONLY FOR HAVING CHILDREN?
What Scripture Actually Shows About Marital Pleasure—and Why the Bible Is Far Less Embarrassed About Married Desire Than Many Christians Are
There are married Christians who can pray together without shame.
They can worship together.
Read Scripture together.
Raise children together.
Serve in church together.
And yet when the bedroom door closes, something strange happens.
They suddenly become embarrassed by something God Himself created.
A husband wonders whether enjoying his wife too much is somehow “carnal.”
A wife has spent years feeling guilty for wanting to be desired.
A couple knows that sex can produce children—but somewhere along the way they absorbed the idea that reproduction must therefore be the only truly holy reason for sexual intimacy.
And sometimes nobody ever explicitly taught them this.
They simply inherited it.
From silence.
From awkwardness.
From shame.

From the strange assumption that holiness requires Christians to speak confidently about adultery, lust, fornication, and sexual sin—but almost whisper when Scripture speaks about the beauty of sexual love inside marriage.
So we need to ask the question plainly:
Is sex only for having children?
And perhaps an even more uncomfortable question:
Does the Bible actually permit a husband and wife to desire, enjoy, and delight in one another sexually—even when conception is not the immediate purpose of their intimacy?
The answer should not come from modern sexual culture.
It should not come from pornography.
It should not come from reactionary purity culture.
It should not come from whatever makes us personally comfortable.
It must come from Scripture.
And once Scripture is allowed to speak for itself, something beautiful emerges:
The Bible honors procreation profoundly, but it does not reduce marital sexuality to procreation.
Children are unquestionably presented as a blessing from God. Genesis establishes the procreative dimension of marriage immediately:
“Be fruitful and multiply.”
In Hebrew:
פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ — perû ûrevû
“Be fruitful and multiply.”
Genesis 1:28.

Human sexuality has an undeniable relationship to fruitfulness. Christianity has no reason to apologize for that. Children are not accidents that interrupt the “real” purpose of marriage. Psalm 127 calls children a heritage from the LORD.
But here is where careful Bible reading matters.
Something may have more than one God-given purpose.
Food sustains life, yet Scripture also allows feasting.
Speech communicates information, yet Scripture also gives us poetry and song.
Marriage can produce children, but Scripture also presents marriage as companionship, covenant union, mutual belonging, comfort, delight—and, yes, sexual pleasure.
Go back to the beginning.
Before sin.
Before shame.
Before adultery.
Before pornography.
Before humanity learned to exploit bodies.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
“One flesh.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not describe the woman merely as a reproductive instrument.
Genesis 2 first presents the crisis of human aloneness:
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
God's answer is relational.
Personal.
Covenantal.
Adam receives someone with whom he can share life.
And his response to Eve is almost poetry:
“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Then Scripture gives us one of the most revealing descriptions of innocent embodied existence anywhere in the Bible:
“And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ — velo yitboshashu
They were not ashamed.
That sentence is breathtaking when you remember where it occurs.
Genesis 2:25 comes before the Fall.
Nakedness existed before shame.
The body existed before lust corrupted the gaze.
Sexual difference existed before sexual exploitation.
Marriage existed before adultery.
Desire itself is not the enemy.
Sin is.
And Christianity does something radically different from both sexual repression and sexual permissiveness.
The world often says, “If you desire it, fulfill it.”
Religious shame can imply, “If you desire it, distrust it.”
Scripture says something far richer:
Desire must be brought under the lordship of God.
Some desires must be denied.
Some desires must be crucified.
Some desires must be redirected.
But some desires can be received with thanksgiving because God Himself placed them within a covenant where they can become expressions of faithful love.
And this is where Proverbs becomes almost impossible to misunderstand.
Proverbs 5 warns a young man against adultery. The chapter does not respond to dangerous sexual desire by commanding him to become sexually indifferent.
Instead, Scripture redirects his desire toward his wife.
Then come words Christians sometimes seem embarrassed to read aloud:
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth…”
And then:
“Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:18–19.
Not pornography.
Not secular romance literature.
Not a modern marriage counselor trying to make Christianity more sexually permissive.
Proverbs.
Wisdom literature.
Scripture.
The Hebrew is striking.
The text uses language of rejoicing, delight, and being continually captivated by marital love.
The sexual imagery is not incidental.
The wife is not being described merely as the potential mother of the husband's future children.
The husband is told to rejoice in her.
To delight in her.
To remain captivated by her love.
Why?
Because biblical holiness is not merely the suppression of forbidden desire.
It also includes the proper celebration of righteous desire.
God does not simply tell the married man where he must not drink.
The imagery of Proverbs 5 tells him to drink from his own cistern.
Faithfulness is not portrayed as lifeless deprivation.
It is covenant delight.
And then there is the Song of Songs.
Perhaps nowhere does our discomfort become more obvious.
Because if marital sexual pleasure were legitimate only when directly oriented toward conception, the Song of Songs would be extraordinarily difficult to explain.
Read it carefully.
The lovers admire each other's bodies.
They long for one another.
They speak of kisses.
Fragrance.
Touch.
Beauty.
Gardens.
Fruit.
Spices.
Longing.
Belonging.
The woman is not merely tolerated as the object of male desire.
She speaks.
She desires.
She initiates.
She longs.
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.”
And later:
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
Song of Songs 7:10.
The Hebrew word translated “desire” there is:
תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah
The Song does not treat mutual marital attraction as something embarrassing that mature believers eventually outgrow.
It places covenantal desire inside biblical poetry.
That does not mean every line of the Song should be crudely literalized. Nor does it settle every theological question Christians have debated about sexuality.
But we should not erase what is plainly present.
The Song celebrates the beauty of love between bride and bridegroom in embodied, passionate language.
And notably, its expressions of desire are not constantly justified by references to conception.
The lovers delight in one another.
That matters.
Because some Christians have unconsciously turned marriage into a place where sex may be technically permitted while pleasure remains spiritually suspicious.
Scripture does not require us to make that move.
Then Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 7 that becomes even more significant when we remember the ancient world in which he wrote.
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
Then:
“For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
The Greek word translated “likewise” is:
ὁμοίως — homoiōs
Likewise.
Similarly.
In the same manner.
Paul establishes reciprocity.
The husband's body belongs, covenantally, to his wife just as her body belongs, covenantally, to him.
That passage has sometimes been horribly misused as though marriage creates permission for coercion.
It does not.
Read Paul's logic carefully.
The command is reciprocal.
Neither spouse is given unilateral selfish ownership while the other becomes an object.
Christian marital intimacy is shaped by mutuality.
And Paul's next instruction is equally revealing:
“Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again…”
Agreement.
Temporary abstinence.
Then reunion.
Why does Paul encourage reunion?
Among his stated concerns is sexual temptation and lack of self-control.
In other words, sexual intimacy within marriage has a purpose beyond conceiving children.
It can serve marital faithfulness.
Mutual giving.
Union.
Protection against temptation.
And embodied intimacy between husband and wife.
Paul does not say:
“Come together again only when you intend to conceive.”
That sentence is simply not in the text.
This does not diminish children.
It simply refuses to make Scripture say less—or more—than Scripture actually says.
Hebrews 13:4 gives us another important boundary:
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled…”
The Greek word translated “bed” is:
κοίτη — koitē
In context, the marriage bed is treated as something that can remain undefiled precisely because sexual immorality is being contrasted with the honorable covenant of marriage.
The Bible therefore refuses two opposite errors.
It refuses to worship sex.
And it refuses to demonize sex.
Outside God's boundaries, sexuality can become profoundly destructive.
Adultery destroys trust.
Pornography trains people to consume bodies rather than love persons.
Lust turns a human being into an object inside the imagination.
Sexual exploitation wounds people God made in His image.
Fornication contradicts God's design for sexual union within marriage.
But the abuse of something does not prove that its proper use is shameful.
Fire can destroy a house.
Fire can also warm one.
The issue is not whether fire exists.
The issue is whether it remains where it belongs.
And this is where the Gospel enters the bedroom in ways many Christians desperately need.
Because maybe your problem is not theological curiosity.
Maybe this article touched a wound.
Maybe sexuality has never felt innocent to you.
Maybe you carry memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe someone crossed yours.
Maybe pornography reshaped your imagination.
Maybe adultery shattered your marriage.
Maybe you were sexually reckless before coming to Christ.
Maybe you were taught that your body itself was dirty.
Maybe your marriage now contains years of rejection, resentment, exhaustion, misunderstanding, physical changes, infertility, trauma, mismatched desire, or silence.
Maybe you are reading an article about marital pleasure while quietly thinking:
You don't know my story.
No.
But Jesus does.
And the Christian message is not that sexually unbroken people get to approach God while everyone else remains permanently stained.
The Gospel is that sinners can be washed.
Paul writes to believers in Corinth after naming serious patterns of sin, including sexual sin, and then says:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified…”
1 Corinthians 6:11.
Were.
That word carries hope.
Your sin may belong to your history without being allowed to own your identity.
What you did matters.
What happened to you matters.
Repentance matters.
Healing matters.
Consequences can be real.
Trust may need rebuilding.
But Jesus Christ is not intimidated by the chapter you wish nobody knew.
At the cross, Christ does not pretend sin is harmless.
He demonstrates how serious it is.
And in His resurrection, He demonstrates that sin and death do not get the final word.
This is why grace is not permission to continue destroying ourselves.
Grace calls us home.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace transforms.
Grace takes sexuality away from both shame and idolatry and places the whole person under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
So, is sex only for having children?
Scripture does not present it that way.
Procreation is a beautiful and significant good associated with marriage and sexual union.
But Scripture also presents marital intimacy in connection with one-flesh union, companionship, mutual belonging, delight, desire, faithfulness, and reciprocal conjugal responsibility.
There is no biblical requirement that married couples feel guilty because they experience pleasure in one another.
But there is also something important that must be said.
Biblical marital pleasure is not selfish consumption with a wedding ring added to it.
Marriage does not baptize selfishness.
A husband does not honor God by treating his wife's body as an entitlement.
A wife does not honor God by treating intimacy as a weapon of manipulation.
Neither spouse should use Scripture to pressure, humiliate, threaten, or coerce the other.
Christlike love asks something deeper:
How can I love you faithfully?
Not merely:
What can I get from you?
Ephesians 5 ultimately places Christian marriage beneath the enormous reality of Christ and His Church.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That is not the language of consumption.
It is sacrifice.
Christ gives Himself.
So Christian intimacy should never become the opposite of Christlike love.
The bedroom is not a theological exemption where selfishness suddenly becomes holy.
Tenderness matters.
Patience matters.
Communication matters.
Consent matters.
Faithfulness matters.
The wellbeing of your spouse matters.
And sometimes love looks passionate.
Sometimes it looks patient.
Sometimes it looks like listening.
Sometimes it means recognizing pain, illness, postpartum recovery, disability, trauma, grief, exhaustion, age, hormonal changes, or emotional wounds that affect intimacy.
A biblical theology of marital pleasure should make husbands and wives more loving, not more demanding.
More tender.
Not more entitled.
More honest.
Not more manipulative.
Because ultimately marriage itself points beyond marriage.
Sex is not God.
Romance is not God.
Your spouse is not your Savior.
Marriage cannot carry the weight of your soul.
Even the happiest marriage on earth is temporary.
Jesus taught that resurrection life cannot simply be reduced to the continuation of earthly marriage as we presently experience it.
Marriage is precious.
But Christ is ultimate.
Sexual pleasure is a gift.
But Christ is the Giver.
Children are a blessing.
But Christ is Lord.
And perhaps that is the freedom somebody needed today.
You do not have to worship sexuality.
You do not have to fear it.
You do not have to call evil what God designed for good.
And you do not have to call good what God calls sin.
You can bring your sexuality—your desires, failures, wounds, marriage, singleness, temptations, memories, questions, and body—to Jesus Christ.
All of it.
Nothing hidden.
Nothing dressed up.
Nothing pretending.
Because Christianity is not the story of people who successfully kept their scandals secret.
It is the story of sinners meeting a Savior whose grace is greater than the identities sin tried to give them.
You can simply write “Christ is still healing me.”
And if grace has already restored something you once thought was permanently destroyed, tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that restoration is possible.
Send it privately to someone who would never publicly admit that this subject has been hurting them.

Supporting Christian ministry should never be presented as though paying money earns God's favor—it does not. Salvation is by grace, and God's glory cannot be purchased. But when you freely choose to support biblical work you believe is bearing good fruit, that generosity can itself become an act of stewardship and participation in Gospel ministry.
And don't keep the message trapped on this page.

One share can reach a marriage you never knew was struggling. One tag can reach someone carrying shame in silence. One honest comment can make another believer realize they are not the only person still fighting. One saved article can become something someone returns to on a difficult night.
But remember this before you leave.
The greatest intimacy you will ever experience is not ultimately found in another human being knowing your body.
It is found in Jesus Christ knowing the darkest rooms of your soul…
and still calling you out of hiding and into His grace.
